strengths: Solid theoretical contributions: Theorem 4.1 provides clear necessary/sufficient conditions for ESP in diagonal case; Proposition 4.2 establishes expressivity equivalence to general linear ESNs with proper diagonalization argument

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse benchmarks (memory-based, forecasting, time series classification) with appropriate baselines (LSTM, Transformer, LRU, Mamba) and statistical significance testing

Significant practical efficiency gains: order-of-magnitude speedups in training time (Fig. 4), ability to scale to 100K+ dimensional reservoirs vs ~10K for traditional ESN, with honest reporting of energy/emissions metrics
Well-executed complexity analysis showing logarithmic temporal complexity via associative scan and linear parameter space complexity via diagonal structure—validated empirically in Fig. 2
Clear presentation with effective architectural visualization; thorough appendix supporting reproducibility including detailed hyperparameters, computational resources, and dataset specifications
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: Core contribution primarily adapts existing techniques (LRU's diagonal recurrence, associative scan from SSMs) to RC rather than introducing fundamental innovations; mixing function design appears ad-hoc without strong theoretical justification

Limited accuracy improvements over baselines: Tables 1-2 show comparable performance to traditional ESN; Table 4 shows 96.2% on sMNIST vs 98.5% for Mamba—the 2.3% gap is non-trivial. Primary value proposition is efficiency, not accuracy

Significant gap between theory and practice: Theorem 4.3 requires non-linear MLP readout for universality guarantees, yet most experiments use linear ridge regression (Tables 1-3). Unclear which theoretical guarantees apply in which experimental settings

Insufficient justification of key design choices: (1) Why 1D convolutional mixing with tanh specifically? (2) Ring topology for deeper layers—rationale and expressivity impact? (3) State concatenation in readout (Eq. 7)—why optimal? (4) Initialization scaling √(1-|λᵢ|²) for complex space—is this optimal?

Critical structural RC comparison (Table 9 showing clear advantages over SCR/Structured RC) relegated to appendix with minimal discussion; this is important for positioning and should be in main paper

Missing ablation studies on component contributions: no analysis of mixing function necessity, impact of ring vs dense topology, effect of alternative mixing designs, or comparison with simpler nonlinearities
Weak analysis of sequence length limitations: Fig. 2 shows speedup advantage diminishes on short sequences (Lorenz25/50), but implications and applicability conditions not thoroughly discussed

Notation and clarity issues: inconsistent notation (h_t vs h_t^(ℓ)), relationship between simplified theoretical model (linear readout in Section 4) and complex practical model (mixing function + MLP) needs clarification
No code availability statement despite strong emphasis on reproducibility; existing baseline references don't include ParalESN itself, limiting practical validation

Limited practical guidance: unclear when ParalESN should be preferred over simpler alternatives (e.g., directly using Mamba); discussion of specific deployment scenarios (edge devices, resource-constrained settings) minimal despite efficiency claims

strengths: Sound theoretical analysis with correct proofs of Echo State Property preservation and universality in fading memory filters
Significant computational efficiency gains (10× speedups, logarithmic time complexity reduction from linear) with rigorous complexity analysis
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse benchmarks (memory, forecasting, classification) with thoughtful efficiency metrics tracking
Well-engineered architecture design with practical memory optimizations (diagonal matrices, 1D convolutional mixing, ring topology)
Clear problem motivation and presentation; good documentation of experimental methodology in appendices
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core components (diagonal linear RNNs via LRU, associative scan, 1D convolutional mixing) are borrowed from existing work without fundamental innovation
Accuracy improvements over traditional ESN are marginal and inconsistent across benchmarks (Table 2 shows similar performance; Table 4 shows 2-3% underperformance vs. LRU/Transformer)

Overstated practical value proposition: claims of 'competitive with fully-trainable models' are misleading given ParalESN achieves 96.2% on sMNIST while LRU achieves 98.5%; no clear guidance on when practitioners should use ParalESN

Theoretical contributions are straightforward applications of existing results (Theorem 4.1 is standard spectral radius analysis, Prop 4.2 is basic eigendecomposition, Corollary 4.3 follows from prior universality results)
Unfair comparison with trained models: untrained/minimally-trained ParalESN (ridge regression) vs. fully-trained LRU/Mamba; no analysis of accuracy-vs-speed at equal computational budget
Mixing function design appears ad-hoc without justification (why 1D convolution? why tanh?) and limited ablation studies on architectural choices
Experimental concerns: hyperparameter search equivalence not established across methods; hyperparameter sensitivity only shown for one task (NARMA10, not MNIST where accuracy gaps are largest)
Missing critical analysis: memory capacity implications of linear recurrence despite universality proofs; practical expressiveness cost of diagonal constraint not discussed

strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse benchmarks (memory-based tasks, forecasting, classification) with proper statistical reporting and fair comparison methodology including modern baselines (LRU, Mamba, Transformer)
Significant practical speedups of 1-2 orders of magnitude and ability to scale to 100K+ dimensional reservoirs where traditional ESN runs out of memory
Solid theoretical analysis with correct proofs of Echo State Property conditions (Theorem 4.1) and expressivity guarantees (Proposition 4.2, Corollary 4.3)
Thoughtful architectural design with memory-efficient choices (ring topology for deep layers, 1-D convolution mixing, complex-valued initialization) that enable parallelization
Clear presentation with excellent figures, well-organized appendix with detailed complexity analysis, proofs, and experimental methodology
Addresses a genuine practical limitation of RC (sequential bottleneck and memory footprint) with a principled parallelization solution via associative scan
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core techniques (diagonal linear recurrence, associative scan) are established in LRU and SSMs; contribution is primarily applying these to RC framework rather than fundamental innovation

Insufficient justification for architectural choices: mixing function (Eq. 6) introduced abruptly without exploring alternatives or ablations; unclear how much it compromises parallelization advantage

Modest accuracy improvements over baselines: on most benchmarks (Tables 1-2), ParalESN shows comparable rather than superior accuracy to traditional ESN, limiting use cases beyond computational efficiency
Deep architecture benefits not thoroughly analyzed: no ablation studies comparing equal-capacity single vs. multi-layer models; unclear whether improvements stem from depth or total capacity increase

Incomplete trade-off analysis: paper doesn't clearly articulate when practitioners should prefer ParalESN over existing alternatives (LRU, Mamba); missing discussion of practical limitations and conditions where method excels

Sensitivity to phase parameters (θ) appears significant (Fig. 6) but investigation is limited; memory capacity claims rely on basic benchmarks without systematic comparison against other structured RC approaches
Reproducibility gaps: no explicit code release commitment, associative scan implementation details missing, parallel execution strategy unclear, complex number handling not fully detailed
